stem: Coins come in denominations `{1, 3, 4}`. A greedy routine always takes the largest coin that still fits. How many coins does it use to make 6, and is that optimal?

options.text: 3 coins (4 + 1 + 1), and that is optimal
options.why: A two-coin answer exists, 3 + 3, so greedy is not optimal here.

options.text: 3 coins (4 + 1 + 1), but 2 coins (3 + 3) is optimal
options.why: Taking 4 first leaves 2, which costs two 1-coins; skipping 4 allows 3 + 3.

options.text: 2 coins (3 + 3), because greedy finds the optimum here
options.why: Greedy starts with the largest coin, 4, so it never builds 3 + 3.

options.text: 2 coins (4 + 2), since 2 can be paid with one coin
options.why: There is no 2-coin denomination; 2 has to be paid as 1 + 1.

explanation: Greedy takes 4, leaving 2, which needs 1 + 1: three coins. But 3 + 3 makes 6 with two coins. Largest-coin-first is only optimal for "canonical" coin systems; for arbitrary denominations you need dynamic programming.

stem: In the fractional knapsack problem you may take any fraction of an item. Taking items in decreasing value-per-weight order, and a fraction of the last one, always gives the maximum total value.

options.text: True
options.why: With fractions there is no wasted capacity, so the best ratio first is always optimal.

options.text: False
options.why: That failure belongs to 0/1 knapsack; splitting items removes the leftover-capacity problem.

explanation: Because fractions are allowed, capacity can always be filled exactly, and every unit of capacity is spent on the best remaining value density. An exchange argument proves it. The same rule fails for 0/1 knapsack, where items can't be split.
reference: CLRS, ch. 16.2: Elements of the greedy strategy

stem: What does `12 & (12 - 1)` evaluate to in Python?

options.why: 1100 AND 1011 is 1000: the lowest set bit is cleared.
That is just n - 1; the AND keeps only bits set in both.
4 is the lowest set bit itself, which `12 & -12` gives.
0 only happens for powers of two; 12 has two set bits.

explanation: 12 is `1100` and 11 is `1011`. ANDing them keeps `1000` = 8. In general `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, which is the basis of the power-of-two check and Kernighan's bit-counting loop.

stem: Every number in `[4, 1, 2, 1, 2]` appears twice except one. Folding the list with XOR (`4 ^ 1 ^ 2 ^ 1 ^ 2`) gives which number? Type the number.
explanation: XOR is associative and commutative, `x ^ x = 0` and `x ^ 0 = x`, so every pair cancels and the single value remains: 4. This finds the unique element in O(n) time and O(1) space.

stem: To schedule the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings in one room, which greedy rule is provably optimal?

options.text: Pick the meeting that ends earliest, then repeat
options.why: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the rest; an exchange argument proves it.

options.text: Pick the meeting that starts earliest, then repeat
options.why: An early, long meeting can block many short ones: (0, 10) versus (1, 2) and (3, 4).

options.text: Pick the shortest meeting first, then repeat
options.why: A short meeting straddling two others blocks both: (4, 7) between (0, 5) and (6, 11).

options.text: Pick the meeting with the fewest overlaps first
options.why: It's a heuristic with known counterexamples, not the rule the proof supports.

explanation: Earliest finish time first is optimal: the chosen meeting ends no later than the first meeting of any optimal schedule, so swapping it in never hurts, and induction finishes the proof. Earliest start and shortest-first both have small counterexamples.

```python
print(gcd(48, 18))
```

stem: Which two problems does a simple greedy rule solve optimally? (Choose two.)

options.text: Fractional knapsack, taking the best value-per-weight first
options.why: Items can be split, so capacity is always filled with the densest value.

options.text: Activity selection, taking the earliest-finishing activity
options.why: Swapping in the earliest finisher never breaks an optimal schedule.

options.text: 0/1 knapsack, taking the best value-per-weight first
options.why: Weights 10/20/30, values 60/100/120, capacity 50: ratio greedy gets 160, but 220 is possible.

options.text: Making change for any coin set by taking the largest coin
options.why: Coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6: greedy uses 3 coins, the optimum uses 2.

options.text: Longest increasing subsequence by always extending with the next larger number
options.why: For [1, 5, 2, 3, 4] it takes 1, 5 (length 2) and misses 1, 2, 3, 4.

explanation: Fractional knapsack (best value density first) and activity selection (earliest finish first) both have greedy-choice proofs. 0/1 knapsack, arbitrary coin change and longest increasing subsequence need dynamic programming.

What does this print?

```python
def can_jump(nums):
    far = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if i > far:
            return False
        far = max(far, i + x)
    return True

print(can_jump([3, 2, 1, 0, 4]))
```

options.text: False
options.why: Every route reaches index 3, whose 0 traps you; far never passes 3.

options.text: True
options.why: Index 4 needs a jump from index 3 or earlier with enough range; none has it.

options.text: IndexError
options.why: The loop only reads valid indices, so nothing goes out of range.
The function returns a boolean, not the farthest reachable index.

explanation: `far` tracks the furthest reachable index. Indices 0–3 all reach at most index 3, and index 3 holds 0, so at i = 4 the check `i > far` (4 > 3) returns False. The greedy is O(n) because reachability only needs the maximum reach so far.

options.why: The greed-1 child is satisfied; a size-1 cookie can't satisfy greed 2.
Both cookies are size 1, so only the greed-1 child can be content.
There are only two cookies, so at most two children could be content.
The size-1 cookie is enough for the child whose greed is 1.

explanation: Sorted, the first size-1 cookie satisfies the greed-1 child. The second size-1 cookie can't satisfy greed 2, so the answer is 1. Giving the smallest sufficient cookie to the least greedy child is optimal by an exchange argument.

stem: Split `"ababcbacadefegdehijhklij"` into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part. The standard greedy extends the current part to the last occurrence of every letter seen so far and cuts when the index reaches that end. What part sizes does it produce?

Cuts must cover each letter's last occurrence, not split evenly.
'defegde' and 'hijhklij' share no letters, so a cut fits between them.
'a' appears again at index 8, so the first part can't end after 'ab'.

explanation: Record each letter's last index, then sweep: the first part must reach the last `a` at index 8 (covering b and c), giving 9. The next runs to the last `e` at 15 (size 7), and the last to the end (size 8). Cutting at the earliest legal point maximises the number of parts.

stem: Balloons span `[[10, 16], [2, 8], [1, 6], [7, 12]]` on the x-axis. An arrow shot straight up at x bursts every balloon whose span includes x (endpoints count). What is the minimum number of arrows needed? Type a number.

stem: Meetings run `[[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]]`. What is the minimum number of meeting rooms needed?

[5, 10] ends before [15, 20] starts, so they reuse one room.
[0, 30] overlaps the other two, so one room is not enough.
There are only three meetings, so four rooms can't be the minimum.

explanation: Sort by start and keep a min-heap of end times: [0,30] takes room 1; [5,10] needs room 2; [15,20] starts after 10, so it reuses room 2. The answer equals the maximum number of meetings overlapping at one instant.


options.text: False

stem: Numbers arrive in an endless stream, and after each one you must report the kth largest value seen so far. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Keep a min-heap of the k largest values seen
options.why: Each update is O(log k) and the heap top is the kth largest.

options.text: Keep every value in a list and sort it after each arrival
options.why: That costs O(n log n) per update and grows without bound.

options.text: Keep a max-heap of every value seen so far
options.why: Finding the kth largest means popping k items, and memory keeps growing.

options.text: Run quickselect on all values after each arrival
options.why: That's O(n) average per update and needs every value in memory.

explanation: A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest values; its top is the kth largest. Each arrival costs O(log k) and memory stays O(k), however long the stream runs.
reference: LeetCode 703: Kth Largest Element in a Stream

O(n³)
O(n log n)

stem:
What does this print?

```python
def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
    if sum(gas) < sum(cost):
        return -1
    tank = start = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
        if tank < 0:
            tank = 0
            start = i + 1
    return start

print(can_complete_circuit([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]))
```

options.why: From station 3 the net gains 3, 3, -2, -2, -2 never drop below zero.
Starting at 0 the tank goes 1 - 3 = -2 immediately.
From 4 the tank is 3, then 1, then -1 at station 1, so it fails.
Total gas 15 equals total cost 15, so a valid start exists.

explanation: Net gains are -2, -2, -2, 3, 3. The tank goes negative at stations 0, 1 and 2, moving the start each time; from station 3 it stays non-negative. Total gas (15) equals total cost (15), so the circuit is possible and the answer is 3.

stem: In `nums = [2, 3, 0, 1, 4]`, each value is the maximum jump length from that index. What is the minimum number of jumps from index 0 to the last index?

options.why: Index 0 → index 1, then index 1 jumps 3 to the last index.
The best route skips index 2 (value 0) entirely.
Index 0 can reach at most index 2.

options.text: It can't reach the end
options.why: Index 1 jumps 3 straight to index 4.

explanation: Jump from 0 to 1 (one step), then from 1 jump 3 to index 4: two jumps. The BFS-style greedy expands the reachable window level by level; landing on index 2 (value 0) would be a dead end.

stem: A CPU must run tasks `A A A B B B`. Identical tasks need a cooldown of `n = 2` units between them; each unit runs one task or idles. What is the minimum number of units?

options.why: A B idle A B idle A B: (3 - 1) × (2 + 1) + 2 = 8.
Each A must be 2 units apart, so six slots are too few.
A and B both occur 3 times, so the last frame holds two tasks.
No idle slot is needed after the final frame.

explanation: The most frequent count is 3, shared by A and B. Frames of size n + 1 = 3: `A B idle | A B idle | A B` → (3 - 1) × 3 + 2 = 8. The answer is max(len(tasks), (maxCount - 1) × (n + 1) + numberWithMaxCount).

stem: Tasks are `A A A B C D E F G` with cooldown `n = 2` (the same task must be at least 2 units apart). What is the minimum number of time units? Type a number.
explanation: The frame formula gives (3 - 1) × (2 + 1) + 1 = 7, but there are 9 tasks, and each unit runs at most one task, so the answer is max(9, 7) = 9. The other tasks fill the idle slots: A B C A D E A F G.

options.why: String order puts '30' before '3'; comparing a+b with b+a puts '3' first.

options.text: "9534330", the largest possible
options.why: Reverse lexicographic order places '30' before '3', so it can't produce this.

options.text: "9534303", the largest possible

stem: Children in a row have ratings. Each child gets at least 1 candy, and a child with a higher rating than a neighbour gets more candy than that neighbour. The standard solution does a left-to-right pass, then a right-to-left pass taking the max. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: For ratings [1, 0, 2] the minimum total is 5
options.why: Candies 2, 1, 2 satisfy both neighbours of the middle child.

options.text: For ratings [1, 2, 2] the minimum total is 4
options.why: Candies 1, 2, 1: equal neighbours don't need equal or more candy.

options.text: Equal-rated neighbours must get equal candy
options.why: Only a strictly higher rating creates a constraint.

options.text: A single left-to-right pass is enough
options.why: It misses decreasing runs: [2, 1] needs 2, 1.

options.text: The right pass can set c[i] = c[i+1] + 1 instead of taking the max
options.why: For [1, 2, 3, 1] that sets c[2] to 2, equal to c[1], breaking the left rule.

explanation: Left pass: `c[i] = c[i-1] + 1` when r[i] > r[i-1]. Right pass: `c[i] = max(c[i], c[i+1] + 1)` when r[i] > r[i+1]. [1, 0, 2] → 2, 1, 2 = 5; [1, 2, 2] → 1, 2, 1 = 4. Equal ratings impose no constraint, and the max keeps the left-pass guarantees.

stem: Symbols occur with frequencies 5, 9, 12, 13, 16 and 45 (100 symbols in total). Using a Huffman code, what is the total encoded length in bits (sum of frequency × code length)?

options.why: It equals the sum of merge weights: 14 + 25 + 30 + 55 + 100.
That's a fixed 3-bit code for 100 symbols, which Huffman beats.
One bit per symbol is impossible with six distinct symbols.
Recheck the merges: 14, 25, 30, 55 and 100 sum to 224.

explanation: Huffman repeatedly merges the two smallest weights: 5+9 = 14, 12+13 = 25, 14+16 = 30, 25+30 = 55, 45+55 = 100. The total encoded length equals the sum of all merge weights: 14 + 25 + 30 + 55 + 100 = 224 bits, versus 300 for a fixed 3-bit code.

"aabb"

stem: You start with capital `w = 0` and may finish at most `k = 2` projects. Project i needs `capital[i]` to start and adds `profits[i]` to your capital. k = 2 lets you finish only two of the three projects.

stem: Trains arrive at `[900, 940, 950, 1100, 1500, 1800]` and depart at `[910, 1200, 1120, 1130, 1900, 2000]` (same order). A train occupies a platform from arrival through departure. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.why: The count of trains present doesn't depend on pairing.

stem: For US coins `{1, 5, 10, 25}`, taking the largest coin that fits always uses the fewest coins.

What does this print?

```python
def fpow(b, e, m):
    r = 1
    b %= m
    while e:
        if e & 1:

        e >>= 1

print(fpow(3, 13, 1000))
```

The function reduces mod 1000 at every multiplication.
27 is 3³; e = 13 multiplies in 3¹, 3⁴ and 3⁸.
729 is 3⁶; the exponent here is 13.

explanation: 13 is 1101 in binary, so the result multiplies 3¹ · 3⁴ · 3⁸ = 3¹³ = 1,594,323, reducing mod 1000 each step: 323. Binary exponentiation takes O(log e) multiplications, and reducing every step keeps numbers small.

stem: Items (weight, value) are (10, 60), (20, 100) and (30, 120). Capacity is 50 and items can't be split. Taking items by best value-per-weight gives 60 + 100 = 160. What is the optimal total value? Type a number.
explanation: Ratios are 6, 5 and 4, so the greedy takes the first two (weight 30) and then can't fit the 30-weight item. Taking (20, 100) and (30, 120) uses exactly 50 for 220. 0/1 knapsack needs dynamic programming.

stem: Why is picking the earliest-finishing compatible interval optimal for activity selection?

options.text: An optimal schedule's first interval can be swapped for it without breaking compatibility
options.why: It ends no later, so everything after still fits; induction does the rest.

options.text: The earliest-finishing interval is always the shortest one, and short intervals leave more room overall
options.why: Earliest end isn't shortest: (0, 2) ends first but (5, 6) is shorter.

options.text: It overlaps the fewest other intervals, so choosing it rules out the least
options.why: It can overlap many intervals; the proof never counts overlaps.

options.text: Greedy tries every ordering of intervals and keeps the best
options.why: That's brute force; greedy commits to one choice per step.

explanation: The exchange argument: let O be optimal with first interval x. The greedy's first interval g finishes no later than x, so replacing x with g keeps O's other intervals compatible and its size unchanged. Applying the same argument to the remaining subproblem proves the greedy optimal by induction.
reference: Kleinberg & Tardos, ch. 4.1: "greedy stays ahead" and exchange arguments

stem: Coins are `{1, 5, 10, 12}`. What is the smallest amount for which "take the largest coin that fits" uses more coins than necessary?

options.why: Greedy: 12 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 coins; optimal: 10 + 5 = 2.
12 + 1 is optimal at two coins.
Greedy fails at 20 (12 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 vs 10 + 10), but 15 fails first.
12 + 12 is optimal, and smaller amounts already fail.

explanation: Greedy for 15 takes 12, then 1 + 1 + 1: four coins, while 10 + 5 uses two. No smaller amount fails (checked against DP). Adding a coin like 12 between canonical denominations is a classic way to break the greedy property.
reference: Kozen & Zaks, Optimal bounds for the change-making problem

stem: Which three greedy rules are provably optimal? (Choose three.)

options.text: Minimise maximum lateness: schedule jobs by earliest deadline first
options.why: Swapping any inversion never increases maximum lateness.

options.text: Minimise total completion time on one machine: shortest job first
options.why: Putting a shorter job earlier reduces the waiting of every later job.

options.text: Interval partitioning: process meetings by start time, reusing the room that frees earliest
options.why: The number of rooms used equals the maximum overlap, a lower bound.

options.text: Weighted intervals: take the highest-value non-overlapping interval first
options.why: One value-10 interval can block two value-6 ones; this needs DP.

options.text: Fewest coins for any denomination set: largest coin first
options.why: Coins {1, 3, 4} make 6 with 3 coins greedily but 2 optimally.

options.text: Longest path in a DAG: always follow the heaviest outgoing edge
options.why: A heavy first edge can lead to a short path; use DP in topological order.

explanation: Earliest deadline first minimises maximum lateness, shortest processing time first minimises total completion time, and interval partitioning by start time (reusing the room that frees earliest) uses the minimum number of rooms. Weighted interval scheduling, arbitrary coin change and longest paths need DP.

stem: Using the two-pass candy rule (each child at least 1; a strictly higher-rated child gets more than that neighbour), what is the minimum total for ratings `[1, 3, 2, 2, 1]`?

options.why: Candies 1, 2, 1, 2, 1: each peak beats only its lower neighbours.
Equal neighbours (2, 2) don't need different counts.
Both peaks need more than their neighbours, so at least 7.
The child rated 3 needs only 2, since both neighbours get 1.

explanation: Left pass: 1, 2, 1, 1, 1. Right pass: index 3 (2 > 1) becomes 2; index 1 (3 > 2) stays 2. Final 1, 2, 1, 2, 1 = 7. The two equal ratings in the middle split the row into independent slopes.

stem: "Sort by weight and add an element if the set stays feasible" is guaranteed optimal when the feasible sets form a matroid (the reason Kruskal's algorithm works). Which problem does NOT have that structure, so this greedy can fail?

options.text: 0/1 knapsack, whose feasible sets are item sets within a weight limit
options.why: A weight limit breaks the exchange property: one heavy item can block two light ones.

options.text: Maximum-weight spanning forest of a graph
options.why: Acyclic edge sets form the graphic matroid, which is why Kruskal works.

options.text: Choosing the heaviest set of linearly independent vectors
options.why: Linear independence is the original matroid example.

options.text: Picking at most k items of greatest total weight with no other constraint
options.why: Sets of size at most k form a uniform matroid; take the k heaviest.

explanation: Matroids require the exchange property: from a smaller feasible set you can always add an element of a larger one. Spanning forests (graphic matroid), linearly independent vectors and "at most k items" (uniform matroid) all satisfy it. Weight-limited item sets don't: one heavy item can block two lighter ones.

This jump-game-II code should return the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index. What does it return for `[2, 3, 1, 1, 4]`, and why?

```python
def jump(nums):
    jumps = end = far = 0
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        far = max(far, i + nums[i])
        if i == end:
            jumps += 1
            end = far
    return jumps
```

options.text: 3: it also counts a jump when i reaches the last index
options.why: Looping over the final index adds one unnecessary jump.

options.text: 2: the window logic is correct and the extra loop step changes nothing
options.why: At i = 4, i == end == 4, so it adds a third jump.

options.text: 4: it adds one jump per index it visits
options.why: It only adds a jump when i reaches the current window end.

options.text: 2 here, but 3 for [2, 3, 0, 1, 4]
options.why: It returns 3 for both inputs: i hits end at 0, 2 and 4.

explanation: The correct loop runs `range(len(nums) - 1)`. Here i also reaches the last index; since `end` is 4 there, `i == end` adds a jump that isn't needed, returning 3 instead of 2. Off-by-one errors at the boundary are the most common bug in window-greedy code.

stem: In the gas-station greedy, when the running tank drops below zero at station i, the next candidate start becomes i + 1. Why can every station between the old start and i be skipped?

options.text: Starting at any of them reaches i with no more fuel, so they also fail by i
options.why: Their prefix from the old start was non-negative, so dropping it can't help.

options.text: Stations before i all have less gas than cost, so none of them can ever be a start
options.why: Some have a surplus; the point is the sum from them to i is still negative.

options.text: The answer is unique, so the first failure rules out all earlier stations
options.why: Uniqueness doesn't explain why those particular stations fail.

options.text: It's a heuristic; the algorithm re-checks them at the end
options.why: It never revisits them; the skip is provably safe.

explanation: From the old start s, every prefix sum up to j < i was non-negative. Starting at some k between s and i drops the non-negative prefix from s to k - 1, so the sum from k to i is at most the (negative) sum from s to i. Every such k also fails by i, so jumping to i + 1 loses nothing.

stem: Put the steps of building a Huffman code in order.

options.text: Count how often each symbol appears
Put every symbol in a min-heap keyed by frequency
Pop the two lowest-frequency nodes and push a parent whose frequency is their sum
Repeat until one node remains: it is the root of the code tree
Read each code by walking from the root, 0 for left and 1 for right

explanation: Huffman coding is greedy: always merging the two least frequent nodes is safe by an exchange argument, because the two rarest symbols can be siblings at the deepest level of some optimal tree. With a heap it runs in O(n log n).
